utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We are here today to have our Pre-Defence Conference in the case against Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic, Prosecutor against Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic. The Pre-Defence Conference we find under Rule 73 ter. The first point on my agenda was to stress a word of welcome to new co-counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He's otherwise engaged, but I shall pass on Your Honours' welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We're glad that apparently the matter of counsel, co-counsel, has been resolved, and I take it then that we'll see Mr. Martin soon in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move on to the second item on my agenda, which is about decisions to be taken in -- under Rule 73 ter. The Stanisic Defence has requested to be allowed to call 33 witnesses in 87 hours, and the Simatovic Defence requested to be allowed to call 20 witnesses in 19 -- 92.5 hours. There are a few uncertainties such as the time needed for the examination of expert witnesses in the Stanisic Defence. They were not included in the 87 hours and -- Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in the process of instructing and having the reports finalised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll deal with the expert reports in a moment. So therefore I'm just pointing in this moment that this uncertainty which appears from your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, and it's difficult for us to provide an estimate. We can try if Your Honours would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware that we have to live with some uncertainties. That is unavoidable, and therefore to now start speculating on whether you would need 3 or 5 or 2.5 or 6 hours with that expert is not something I think would greatly assist the Chamber in making the determinations it has to make. We have carefully looked at the submissions, and we have looked at the summaries of the witness statements, the time estimates for needed -- the time needed for examination-in-chief of those witnesses. Of course, we have also looked at whether these would be 92 ter, 92 bis witnesses. We have given it full consideration, and at this moment the Chamber is inclined to determine that the number of witnesses would be accepted by the Chamber but that both the Stanisic Defence and the Simatovic Defence would be granted 70 hours to present their cases. When I'm talking about 70 hours, then I'm talking about 70 hours examination-in-chief of the witnesses which appear on the list. But before making any final determination in this respect, the Chamber would like to invite the views of the Defence if the Chamber would thus decide, and if the Prosecution would like to make any further comments on it, although it not perhaps being the primary concern of the Prosecution, of course, they can do so as well. Who would be the first to give any comments if there is any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- we would prefer to be able to make written submission on the issue, and we would also prefer if it's possible if Your Honours would be able to provide some guidance as to how Your Honours arrived at that reduction. Only then it seems would we be able to address them - excuse me - specifically. Obviously, if Your Honours want me to deal with it now, I will, but in the absence of understanding precisely why Your Honours came to that conclusion, it's difficult. We took what we thought was a conservative approach, and we thought it was conservative because of the breadth of this indictment and the volume of evidence the Prosecution had called, and we attempted to nonetheless direct our defence at the issues we think are the live issues, and we would submit that much of what the Prosecution have led is not, but that was our reasoning. I can expand on the point in relation to specific witnesses if Your Honours wish, but our preference would be able to do it in writing if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, of course, there's a bit of a problem in Rule 73 ter, unless you're asking for further delays, which says: "After having heard the Defence, the Trial Chamber shall determine the time available to the Defence for presenting evidence." I mean, that's what we're supposed to do during this 60 -- 73 ter Pre-Defence Conference. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent there would be any misunderstanding, perhaps there is not, that when I'm talking about 70 hours, it's 70 hours for the Stanisic Defence and 70 hours for the Simatovic Defence, but that is understood, I take it. Apart from that, Mr. Jordash, I told you that Rule 73 ter requires that once we have heard the Defence, that the Trial Chamber shall determine the time available to the Defence for presenting evidence, and this Chamber thought it wise to give you an impression on what our preliminary thoughts were on the basis of the written submission, which would allow you to better make any comments. Of course, we could go into all kind of details, not to say that the Chamber has not certain questions but just to -- at the same time, we also know that this is not mathematics on from the beginning. I mean, one plus one is two, that's clear, but whether you need one hour or 50 minutes or 65 minutes for a witness, of course, is a matter of -- I would say kind of a mixture between experience, observation on how time was used during the Prosecution's case. Just to take one example where there still would be a possibility for some discussion. We saw in a submission by the Prosecution that they, for example, had not a clear idea on what - and think it was one of the witnesses proposed by you - what they could expect from -- to hear from Mr. Blewitt, for example, that at least the Prosecution sought for further clarification of that, which brought a totally different question to the Chamber's mind, is has there ever been any discussion between the Prosecution and the Defence on whether they could agree on any fact you would elicit from Mr. Blewitt as a witness? If there would be -- I would say if there would be any witness which might be someone who would give information to which the Prosecution perhaps could easily agree, that might be Mr. Blewitt, who is one of the former employees of the Prosecution. So, therefore, one of the things that comes to our mind is has this been discussed, and if not, why not, and would it not save time if you would agree on these matters? I don't know. Just a simple question. Did you discuss this with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, in a sense, yes, in that we contacted the Prosecution, first of all, for consent to contact Mr. Blewitt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We gave our reason for that and what we hoped he would be able to confirm, and then we sent an e-mail to Mr. Blewitt through the Prosecution. So the issue that we want Mr. Blewitt to address is there and it has been communicated to the Prosecution. So we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. What you say is, "They didn't invite us to agree on any matter," but you did not invite them to agree on any matter either. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I'm not -- I'm not blaming the Prosecution for not responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's equally at -- both sides are at fault for not being [indiscernible], but we do blame the Prosecution for suggesting they don't know what Mr. Blewitt was expecting to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's not -- that was just, I would say, the link to my question rather than -- but, of course, one of the questions is also looking at what -- what the kind of issue is you would like to -- to go through with Mr. Blewitt, it should be at least given an attempt to see whether there could be any agreement on the matter, because it seems that, at least from what I see, is that these are relatively objective, factual-seeking, not the facts you would consider the first to be highly contentious. So therefore, then, we ask ourselves why would we spend time on a witness who comes from far away if not at least an attempt has been made to see whether the information you expect to elicit from that witness could be facts on which you would easily agree. Now, that's -- of course, as I said before, there are -- we are living with some uncertainties, but, of course, we went through all of the material, and we made an assessment, as I said on the basis of past experience, on the basis of the information you've provided there. Not to say that if in the future you would be able to clearly demonstrate that assessment was wrong, that that could under no circumstances be corrected, but if you were asking us to give us the considerations we based our assessment upon, it is mainly your submissions, and then, of course -- again, it's not mathematics here, as you are aware of, as everyone is aware of. So therefore, if you say, "We'd like to make submissions in writing," at this moment under 73 ter that would cause at least some problems. So if there's anything you would like further explain at this moment you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will very briefly address the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just an example. You're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The first 18 witnesses are in some way the most substantial and substantive, and we made a decision to try to keep the number of witnesses down and to keep the witness list short, but to have witnesses who could testify to a breadth subjects, and that is what the first 18 witnesses attempt to do. We have tried in that list to cover the principal subjects as we see them, the structure of the DB, the Krajina -- or Croatian crime base, and the Bosnian crime base, and also the Red Beret subject. The indictment is broad. It is broad in terms of time. It's broad in terms of geographical locations, and it is broad in -- in the sense that the Prosecution have adduced thousands of pages of evidence through 92 ter. Almost every substantive witness that the Prosecution called, and there was substantially more than what we are attempting to call, came with in most times 40 -- up to 40 or 50 exhibits, some of them 10, 20, and up to a hundred pages long, and previous testimony from previous trials at the ICTY and often several statements. We can't match that, because we haven't got time to take 92 ter statements of that kind of length. With the best will in the world, with the time we were given - and we're not complaining about that - but with the best will in the world, we would could not possibly have taken 92 ter statements for our witnesses except for one or two, and we would hope to be able to attempt that with some more of the witnesses over the next few months. But in short, the Prosecution case is big and it's detailed, and it makes tens, or, rather, hundreds of allegations which we have to analyse and work out which ones we really need to meet, and we've tried to do that, and our witnesses we believe do do that, but these witnesses will need to cover a range of topics. If I take DST-31, a witness who was close to Babic and -- and, Your Honours will know that the Prosecution -- that Prosecution witness has statements and testimony which run into the hundreds of pages. We want to call DST-31, and we want to lead him in evidence for four to five hours. If the one calculates the length of time that that Prosecution witness gave evidence, it would come to significantly. In order to meet that allegation or that series of allegations made by Babic and made by the other witnesses the Prosecution called in relation to the Krajina, we need a minimum of time, and in our respectful submission, the estimates we've given for the Krajina witnesses, for example, witnesses 427, a total of approximately 6, 7, to 18 or 19 hours, is way, way, way less than the Prosecution's corresponding evidence which was submitted through 92 ter, and so in our submission, the estimates are conservative. I could make the same point, and I will -- will -- and I do make the same point in relation to the other witnesses. It's very difficult to meet paper evidence which comes in the hundreds and thousands of pages without the benefit of the time to apply pursuant to 92 ter. It's difficult it do that without the minimum of time. DST -- staying with DST-31, he will cover from late 1990. His evidence will focus on 1991, and it will move through the military and political events with emphasis on the former throughout 1991 and into 1992. In our submission, four to five hours is about right, and actually probably a bit less, but we tried to factor in concerns which we knew Your Honours would have about timing. In relation to the witnesses we've tried to or we want to call for a longer period, DST-30 and DST-42 and DST-40, these are perhaps the biggest witnesses in terms of the subject matters they cover and the length of time that their evidence will cover. Your Honours can see why, perhaps, they -- we consider them the biggest witnesses. It's very difficult to address a Prosecution theory which expands from 1991 to 1995 without witnesses such as these who present an overview of topics. Again, we submit, that is a conservative estimate, and you can see with DST-40, we've -- we're mindful of the fact that that witness could, if we don't try to -- or attempt to put that witness into 92 ter form, we really wouldn't be able to complete that witness in anything less than probably eight or nine hours. So I think those are the points I'd like to make. We would -- or we will certainly endeavour to utilise 92 ter. We hope that over the summer we'll be able to achieve that with at least one witness and hopefully up to three witnesses more and that will shortcut things we hope. Those are the submissions I would make at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we -- could the Simatovic Defence also comment on what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do so, of course -- it was clear to the Chamber that whereas the number of witnesses you propose is lower, that of course a substantial part of the time taken in the case presentation is covered by the time you'd need to call Mr. Simatovic as a witness in his own case. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Good afternoon to everyone, and thank you for giving me the floor. As far as our time estimate is concerned, for the most part it tallies with what our learned friend Mr. Jordash said concerning the scope of the indictment and the fact that it covers a period of five years as well as two states, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. There's also the fact that the number of witnesses is great, as well as the amount of material put forth by the Prosecution in their case. On top of that, I'd also add another fact which I believe Mr. Jordash did not explore sufficiently in his address. That is to say that there are statements under Rule 92 ter where we have three important witnesses and a large amount of material concerning those witnesses. There is also some other material under 92 quater. It's a lot of material and a lot of time that it requires as well as that there is a lot of territory that we wish to cover in our case. First I wanted to say this, and I hope it will be broached later as well, that this Defence attempted to persuade the Chamber, as well as -- the Trial Chamber as well as the Appeals Chamber to be accorded more time given the facts that we have and the time we need to launch our case. I agree that we may not have been fully successful in providing sufficient quality arguments to persuade both Chambers of the necessity to be accorded sufficient time to prepare ourselves. However, this Defence did not wish to calculate, to try to buy more time, and we did our utmost to conclude all investigations to date. However, we were unable to. We still have a number of things on our list that need to be verified in the field, and we will strive to be efficient. The time we were given and the time we estimated in view of the number of witnesses is something that we believe is necessary in order to address adequately the evidence and allegations the Prosecutor put forth against our client, and we believe that in that light, the number of witnesses we proposed is necessary. I must say that the time allocated to us was a limiting factor, and we couldn't work on many 92 ter statements, because it would require a lot of time for every single witness. As you saw, we decided instead to have viva voce testimony. During an analysis that Mr. Petrovic and I conducted, we realised that the time we estimated for our viva voce witnesses does not go over the time that we would otherwise need to hear the witnesses according to 92 ter. I'll be completely honest, Your Honour. Perhaps we did some things on purpose so as not to be put in the -- in a situation which we would have to ask you for additional time for each and every witness, and we may have reserved some additional time in our initial estimates, but what I'm trying to say now is that now there's a number of additional potential witnesses. I won't speculate with any numbers, but we are considering another dozen or up to 15 witnesses whom we now have to get in touch with. We will try to include that time within the time we initially sought, although we might be forced to ask for a bit of additional time. Irrespective of the fact that some parts of the indictment are common to all -- to both the accused, it would be fair to both of them to be given at least the amount of time used by the Prosecution in the presentation of their case. So as not to repeat what Mr. Jordash has already said, which is something that goes for both the accused, I just wanted to say that we believe that the time we provided in our 65 ter list is the time necessary for us to carry out our work with due diligence. In the time we estimated, we also concluded two expert witnesses. We know from experience before this Court that expert testimony is usually longer than the testimony of fact witnesses. These two witnesses will take up 15 hours in total, I believe. As far as we could see, the Stanisic Defence would not have such experts of that type. That is why we believe it necessary to bring such witnesses before you and the time we need for their testimony ought to be included in the time allocated to us. There's nothing else that I wish to add with regard to the issue of necessity to bring all those witnesses and that they be given the time we asked for. I am not sure Mr. Jordash broached that topic in detail. The accused Franko Simatovic, in addition to all the locations of crimes and facts relating to those locations, we also had witnesses which addressed Mr. Simatovic's relationships, say, with the Serb Volunteer Guard of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and other bodies and people. These things remain to be cleared up, and we believe it is necessary for us to respond by hearing witness testimony. Given the time, we were definitely not in a position to work on our 92 ter statements. We will consider doing so with some of the witnesses, but we also believe that 92 ter statements would not amount to saving much time. As regards the estimated viva voce testimony, we also -- we only took into account those topics which are necessary to show you why we call certain witnesses. We did not wish to expand, and each witness will specifically address only those facts and knowledge they have regarding the accused Simatovic, concerning a specific event, location, or a statement of any of the witnesses that the Prosecution put forth. This is all I wanted to say at the moment, Your Honour, and I apologise beforehand if this fails to meet your need for further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I would have one question for you. You said while it would be reasonable to grant, at least for each accused, the same time as the Prosecution has used for presenting its case. Could you give us examples of not the accuseds' cases before this Tribunal where every accused got the same amount of time as the presentation of the Prosecution's case as a whole. Because that's what you're claiming. I'm seeking whether there's any support to be found in the practice of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm a bit taken aback. I really didn't did not expect to you ask me that, so for time being I can just tell you about my personal experience. This is my fourth time that I appear as Defence counsel. In the first two cases, there was a single accused involved. The third one was the Kosovo case. It is true that in the Kosovo case not all of us were allocated the same amount of time as the Prosecution -- or, rather, we had less time -- or, rather, not each and every Defence got as much time as the Prosecution did. I agree with you on that. However, for example, in the Kosovo case the accused Lukic had received more time than the Prosecutor, I think, because he was in a special situation. He was the only one who was accused from police structures. I believe that you are more familiar with jurisprudence than I am, and if that did exist somewhere in case law, you would have certainly alerted me to that. However, I think that that was not the case until now, but still that does not necessarily mean that I should not think that it would be fair for the accused Simatovic to get the same amount of time that the Prosecutor got for their case, with all due respect. I did not study all of this. I believe that you are more familiar with all of this, and I believe that it's going to be hard for us to find an example of this kind. However, the very fact that there were no such examples until now, with all due respect, does not make me think that it would not be necessary for this to be done in this specific case in view of the very specific circumstances involved in this particular case, that is, with the Defence of the accused Simatovic. Taking all of this into account, I think it would be fair for Simatovic to get at least get those 90 hours that we had envisaged, and that was roughly the amount of time that the Prosecution had for their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simatovic for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will use the first break to consider whether the submissions by the Simatovic and the Stanisic Defence cause us to take more time or to decide that -- either that we stick to the preliminary assessment we've made or whether we would change that, so, therefore, the parties will hear further after the first break how we will proceed in that respect. But where I earlier announced that the Prosecution would have a possibility to -- to address the Chamber in relation to these matters, if they would wish to do so, Mr. Groome, you have that opportunity now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no specific submissions with respect to the time allocated for either Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Then whether or not we'll decide today and what our decision would be if we would decide today, you'll hear that after the first break. I move to another item on the agenda, which is scheduling. And, of course, the scheduling, I couldn't say that it could never be impacted upon by a decision on the total of the time, but that is unlikely in view of the details that we'll discuss at this moment. We sent an e-mail to the parties and that's hereby -- yes, to the parties, and that's hereby put on the record that an e-mail of the 16th of May expressed that the Chamber would like to hear both opening statements on the 15th of June, that is, tomorrow, and that the Chamber should be informed if this would cause any problems. The Stanisic Defence then sent an e-mail expressing its wish to have two hours available for its opening statement, and the Simatovic Defence e-mailed requesting that its opening statement be postponed. The Chamber then instructed the Simatovic Defence to file their request and shortened the deadline for responses. The request and the Prosecution's response were filed on the 2nd and the 3rd of June respectively, and on the 8th of June, the Chamber informed the parties that a request to postpone the opening statement was denied. Now, the reasons for that decision will follow. However, the opening statements are expected to be given tomorrow. Now, Mr. Bakrac, we have no time estimate for you. If -- if we start with a thinking of three and a half effective hours a day where Mr. Jordash asked for two hours, the Chamber wondered whether we could hear both opening statements in one session, which would, if you would divide it equally, which would cost Mr. Jordash 15 minutes out of the two hours he asked for, but we have no indication yet from you. Could you please tell us how much time you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not going to be necessary. I expected you to ask that, and I had intended to provide information to the Court in good time. We consulted the accused, and I've already said that we have not completed our investigation yet. In that situation, we believe that it would not be right for us to make an opening statement. Your Honour, with all due respect, from the point of view of this particular aspect, I did look at the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, and I saw that when there were several accused persons involved in a case, the opening statements were usually made when the actual defence case of each and every individual started. That was the case in Kosovo, Bosanski Samac, and so on. So in case law, we can find quite a few examples of that situation; namely, that the Defence of an individual accused would give its opening arguments at the beginning of their own case. I appreciate the fact that the Trial Chamber looked at our request and our arguments and refused to allow us to give our opening statement at the beginning of our own case, so with due respect, I say that in that situation our Defence has given up on an opening statement altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, have you also used -- looked at the case law where which specific reasons a request for postponement of an opening statement was denied? Could you tell the Chamber now what were the reasons sometimes for not allowing the postponement of an opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to be quite frank. I checked the situations when it was allowed. I did not check the other situations, so I can do that during the break and then respond. I really would not want this position of ours to be misinterpreted by the Trial Chamber. We fully understand that you have your own position that you presented; namely, that our arguments are not sufficiently strong. Therefore, the assessment of our Defence is that an opening statement is not compulsory, so in this situation when we have not fully completed our investigation, our assessment is that it is better for us not to give an opening statement. Perhaps after the Stanisic case we would have to change our original opening statement if we were to give one once our own investigation is completed too; that is to say, when we would be supposed to start our own Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I earlier indicated that the reasons for our decision would follow, and that usually means that we have given it quite some thought and that we'd like to explain to the parties why it exactly was that we denied your request postponing an opening statement, and I'm not giving the full reasons, could have an impact on the fairness of one party towards the other. If you could adapt your situation once you had heard the case presentation by the Stanisic Defence, the Stanisic Defence would not have a similar possibility to do the same. It may have some consequences, for example, for the Prosecution, not knowing what your case is. And if you do not make an opening statement, of course, that would be to some extent the same, would -- could cause some problems for the Prosecution as well when cross-examining Defence witnesses during the Stanisic case presentation. We've given it quite some thought, and that's the reason why I asked you whether you had also looked at the cases where it was not allowed, because that gives a balanced view on what the case law before this Tribunal is. We do therefore understand that in view of the circumstances that you would not make an opening statement at the beginning of the case of the Defence, and that includes both Defence. Mr. Jordash, this also means that there's no major problem in using the two hours you've asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to express my concern that there was a pre-trial brief filed by the Simatovic Defence, the initial Mr. Jovanovic, and there's been some language in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've -- I take it that you're now referring to what you already put on paper: That you have some concerns about a case shifting, the Simatovic Defence saying that they do not have the same concept any more, and that it's unclear to you what that exactly means. You've put that on paper already, I think in your request for -- I don't know exactly where it was. For having an opportunity to -- to reply or I think reply to the -- to the response given by the Simatovic Defence on your urgent motion for -- or is the place wrong, but I remember that I've read some concerns expressed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We have, Your Honour. And I don't intend to repeat them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Other than to point out, if there is no opening now and if the original pre-trial brief is disavowed, the requirements of 65 ter (F) require that the Defence set out at least in general terms the nature of the accused's defence, and I believe that's an obligation that cannot be postponed. Both the Prosecution and Stanisic Defence have the right to know, at least in general terms, what the nature of the accused's Defence is so that we can prepare our examinations of the witnesses during the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see what -- what you're saying is that Rule 65 ter (F) requires the Defence to set out the -- what the nature of the Defence, and if there are changes, you say, apart from whether you make an opening statement or not, that the Prosecution would be entitled to know that there is another -- that the accused's defence has changed and therefore the nature of the accused's defence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that you are entitled to be informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the Prosecution has pointed at several places where you say, well, that is what Mr. Jovanovic may have thought, but we have different concepts. We have a different opinion that -- we find that in various places, including, for example, your choice of an expert, where you say, well, it may be that it fitted into the concept of Mr. Jovanovic, but it does not fit into our concept of Defence any more, which at least suggests that the pre-trial brief may not be valid in every respect any more since it was filed. Could you please respond to the concerns, because you'd just expressed it as a concern. I'm not asking for any relief, Mr. Groome. Could you briefly address that concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you once again for giving me the floor. I understand your concern, however, I assure you that there is no cause for concern. It would be a thankless job now in this point of view to say something about our late colleague and about his pre-trial brief. We want to be very proper. We want to take a humane position with regard to this. If I understand the trial brief -- pre-trial brief correctly, it means challenging the allegations from the indictment. It was my understanding -- again I do apologise. I don't want this to sound very rigid or uncollegiate or improper in view of our late colleague. I understood it as a mere denial of the charges. From that point of view, we don't want to change that. We totally denied the charges in the indictment ourselves. We denied his participation in JCE, any links with the immediate perpetrators, his links with the possible participants in some enterprise, and the Defence is going to remain on those lines. Perhaps we did not formulate our position very skilfully, but even as far as the expert is concerned, it is not our concept that is being changed substantially. This - how do we put this? - the previous expert had missed the point altogether. The question of police expertise is so broad, Your Honour, that volumes and volumes can be written about that. So what we want to achieve through our expert is for him to focus on some other points compared to those that the previous expert had focused on. Again, I do apologise in advance to the expert if he is listening to this. We were not pleased with the concept or the way in which this was presented or with the clarity of the presentation. Quite simply, my colleague Mr. Petrovic and I assessed that working with this expert would involve a new expertise altogether, and the question remains how much we would obtain in terms of what we really want to obtain. Therefore, we believe that with the new expert we are going to focus a great deal more on the key points of our defence and the key topics too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I think that at this moment we do not need a full explanation as why you changed experts in this respect. The concern, you said your concern, addressing me but it was mainly the concern expressed by Mr. Groome, the concern was not necessary. To be quite honest, looking at the language you used, and you said may have been a bit unfortunate language and not expressing exactly what you meant, I think it leaves still some questions open, but rather than elaborate on them in the abstract for hours and hours, perhaps we should closely look at what we will hear from you in the near future. We'll consider whether or not we would invite you, but I'll first have to discuss this with my colleagues, to update us on the Rule 65 ter (F), whether there are any real changes in the nature of the Defence of Mr. Simatovic. We might need to re-read for those purposes, and perhaps the Prosecution could do so as well, the -- the pre-trial brief. And, of course, it's a bit perhaps too simple to say, "Well, the pre-trial brief denied all the charges. We're still doing that and therefore there's no change." That might and bit too superficial an approach to deal with the matter as the matter which is of some concern to Mr. Groome. I do not intend to further deal with this matter at this moment in length. The next scheduling item I wish -- I hope to be able to discuss before the break is about the first witnesses for the Stanisic Defence. We do understand that -- and, Mr. Jordash, whenever there would be any need to go into private session, you'll let me know. We do understand that the situation is such that you do not feel free, rightly or not, but to disclose statements taken from the next two witnesses schedule to appear at this moment. That might change over the days to come. I would to -- because you're asked, as a matter of fact, for -- upon a very practical basis to -- to delay the testimony of the first two witnesses until the 21st of June rather than to hear their testimony starting on the 16th of June, and the Chamber has asked for the parties' views on this request. The Prosecution was neutral, and the Simatovic Defence has not responded. And then on the 8th of June, the Chamber denied the request, and we have considered that court time should be used to the fullest extent possible. You then informed us that you had other difficulties as well, and we invited you to explore the possibility of if you couldn't present these first -- or the first two witnesses for the reasons you've given, whether you could present any other witnesses. Now, you then informed us that you could not produce any witness for this Thursday, the 16th of June, and you proposed to make up for lost time next week. The Chamber considered it of no use to force you into this Thursday. That would not serve any purpose, but nevertheless, when could you realistically present your first witness, because that's whether the initial two scheduled or any other witness, and I'm now thinking in terms of what would happen then not this Thursday but next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: First of all, could I apologise for effectively not being able to follow Your Honour's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question in this respect. When were the statements taken from the two witnesses that were first on your list to be called?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The exact dates when they were completed I don't know off the top of my head, but they were finished I think in -- from the witness's satisfaction last week. The statements have been taken over a period of weeks starting, I think -- three to four months ago I think I started interviewing the first two witnesses, and then obviously there was a process and the witness took away the statement and looked at them, and eventually last week they were completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I do understand that the request for consent by the governments to use the statements is pending already for four weeks --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which means that you can make such an application even without knowing yet the final -- the content of the statement as it's finally is put on paper, because that I take it from your information that the request for consent was filed or submitted four weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Four weeks, as it turned out, was a slight exaggeration on my part. I found the exact date, which was the 24th of May, but our investigator had contacted the National Council a month before that, and the National Council told us that permission would be granted within two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if the statement was not yet completed, they would do that -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. We were asked to send a list of topics that we wanted the witnesses to testify about and that's what we've done. They haven't seen the statement and they haven't requested to see the statement. They simply wanted a list of subjects which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which raises even more questions about the role of this kind of consent in -- but I'm not intending at this moment to engage in a debate on -- on that matter or to invite the parties to have a debate on that. Let's -- let's look at reality at this moment; that is that, at this moment, the consent has not been given yet. I do understand that a possibility for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We were assured it would -- well, I won't say "would," but it was likely to happen tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, not tomorrow, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I am talking about Thursday, but I was not very precise. Could you tell us, do you have the two scenarios, the one in case you would get a consent and the other scenario in case the consent would not be given, because that's what we are interested in, is what will happen next week in either of the two scenarios.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We will do our best to make sure that there's no further delay, and if permission isn't granted on Thursday, and we, expect it will be, then we will get a witness somehow, if we can, to court on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at what moment in time do you then think you could disclose the -- well, either of the statements taken and the supporting material to the extent not yet in the possession of the Prosecution? Would that be on that same Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, all the supporting -- if -- if supporting material are exhibits, then all of the exhibits are in the possession of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but do they know what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. They've had that since last week, an indication of which exhibits will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Used with those --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Used with -- well, with the first witness we've got that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the second witness I think they'll be receiving today or tomorrow the next list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the statements taken from those witness would be available --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On Thursday we can file immediate Rule 92 ter motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you have no alternative scenario in case your expectation would turn out to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in accordance with --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Not as yet worked out, but we will make sure we have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- yes, Ms. Marcus. I see that you're on your feet. I would like -- first of all, you have now received, I take it, relevant information. I don't know whether you were aware of it yet or not. At the same time, we -- there is a 9th of June urgent motion for compliance. The Stanisic Defence has responded to that, and the Prosecution has, I think today, asked whether they could reply to that response. The Chamber has considered that, and if you would like to reply, you have an opportunity to do it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. We have - as Your Honour has pointed out - we have made our submissions in -- in writing in a leave to reply. I don't see any need in detail to go into it again, except with respect to -- to clarify that the notice that we have -- we've been in very regular e-mail contact with the Stanisic Defence team. With respect to the notice that they've given us of the documents for the first witness, there were, as far as we could tell, and there has been some conflicting information, that's one of the problems with all of this, is that some of the e-mails don't match, the spreadsheets don't match, and it's very, very time consuming to try to sort through the variety of information that we've received. We've received notice of 119 potential exhibits, approximately. There are a serious numbers of exhibits not translated into English noticed for the first witness. If I am -- if my numbers are accurate -- and we did receive an e-mail this morning with a few translations, we have not been able to sit down and associate them. One of the problems is that the information is provide to us in a variety of means. Some is uploaded into e-court, some attached to an e-mail, some is in an Excel spreadsheet, et cetera. So we are missing a large number of translations for those documents. We also find that approximately 36 of those 119 documents are redacted, and we haven't seen any motions seeking the unredacted versions. So we do have a number -- a number of concerns. Our last estimate of the untranslated pages is 400 -- 256 pages amongst those documents that have no translation. Now, as I said, we did get an e-mail this morning with a few documents attached. Perhaps some of those translations do address that, but we have not had the opportunity to cross-reference it. So the -- the Defence provided an updated revised notification on the 10th of June that attempts to correct their earlier one, but some of the information in that didn't cross-check either. We've spent enormous resources trying to sort through the conflicting information we've received. All -- all told, in spite of perhaps best efforts on their part, I'm afraid that we -- we are not clear exactly on what exhibits they plan to tender, what the status is of the untranslated exhibits, and that is with respect to the first witness and the witnesses thereafter and, more broadly, with respect to the Defence 65 ter exhibit list. With -- with respect to any statements, we have not received any statements of any witnesses for the Stanisic team, whether a statement be a formal signed statement or an unsigned statement. We've made our position clear: That our understanding of the disclosure obligations under -- Rule 67(A)(2) obliges the Defence to provide us with those statements and that any waiver that may need to be obtained is quite apart from a disclosure obligation to the Prosecution. We've made that also clear in our written submissions that that's our position. And finally, Your Honours, I would point out that to the extent that any of the noticed exhibits are meant to be associated to any statement, we certainly have not been -- we have not received any indication that any of the noticed exhibits are associated, nor as I have said have we received this statement to which they would supposedly be associated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This was a reply, sur-replay for you, Mr. Jordash, and I'm wondering how you work on the basis of untranslated documents for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what the Prosecution have just said is just not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Firstly, and this was copied to your legal officers on Monday, we supplied a list of the exhibits that will be tendered with this witness to the Prosecution. It is clear - I've got it in front of me - there were pages which were not translated. They can be divided into two. One were pages which were not translated because they're parts of Rules and we don't seek to rely upon that section of the Rules, a practice adopted and used by the Prosecution on countless exhibits. Secondly, there were outstanding translations. We can't do much about that but keep pressing the Translation Unit. We have supplied this morning the remaining translation but two. They've been clearly marked and indicated to the Prosecution, and it is not correct that there is or should be any confusion. We agree that when we filed the list there were things which were unclear. Our Case Manager has worked night and day to resolve those things. However, the amount of confusion is exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You say the problem is not as big as --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The problem doesn't exist any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that a cup of tea together with Ms. Marcus will certainly help you out, and then we'll hear from you who starts crying at the end and who is laughing at the end. I hope you're both laughing at this moment. You are doing, as a matter of fact. Redactions was another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The redactions is a problem and we acknowledge that. It's a problem of -- again, it's not of our making. The National Council have been approached by us and they've responded to us and having spoken to BIA, the successor of the DB, and their position appears to be that they want the DB documents to be used in a closed session and they refuse to unredact the sections of the report on the basis that they say the concealed material has nothing to do with this case. We received the letter two weeks ago, and I've just come into possession of the letter. We can -- it's not been translated into English as yet. We can -- it has been sent to the translation unit and we can provide it to my learned friends and Your Honours as soon as we receive a translation. The position would seem to be that either the Serbian government applies for protected measures for those redacted sections, or I think the position of the Prosecution is that we should apply to Your Honours to have that material unredacted. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then that would mean that you make an application for an order to the Serbian government to provide unredacted copies to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's what the Prosecution's preference is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Ms. Marcus is nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the other alternative is that the Prosecution, if they want to see that material, they apply for an order for an unredaction because we don't seek to rely upon what's under -- we understand the Prosecution's concern and we would have the same concerns, but we don't seek to rely upon the material which is hidden. It's not part of our case and we're not concerned with what's under there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say the wish to know more about the context is the Prosecution's wish rather than yours at this moment, and it doesn't make you feel any uncertain on those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I'm always nervous about things which are hidden, but at the same time, I'm -- given that we want to move forward, I'm happy to proceed without.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Mr. Jordash has pointed out, we strenuously object to documents with redactions being used in court let alone tendered. Those are documents that are put forward by the Stanisic Defence. They are their documents, their exhibits. It's our view that any document that they seek to use in court or put to a witness is incomplete without knowing what's underneath the redactions which could clearly impact very seriously on -- on the evidence, and therefore we -- we are -- we are -- we are sticking to our submission quite strongly that we would oppose even the using of -- the use of any of those documents in redacted form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you would say in that case it would be incumbent upon the Stanisic Defence to seek the unredaction of those portions because you would oppose admission into evidence of the redacted versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have three ways now to get out of the problem. None of these would give us a result by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. Our preference would be so we don't lose time, I mean to say -- again, it's not -- it's not a novel situation. We were, on several occasions, from our view hampered or potentially hampered by things which we didn't know, translations which had not been completed and so on. And it's the way it sometimes has to work until these things are resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the parties have now made further submissions, and I linked them to the 9th of June urgent motion, but it also takes it's place in the scheduling of the case. I think we first should take a break now and resume at 5 minutes past 4.00. Is 30 minutes enough or a cup of tea? Yes, okay. Then we resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for resuming so late. The reason was that we wanted to thoroughly discuss the submissions made by the parties in relation to the determinations we have to make under Rule 73 ter, and I will inform you about the outcome. The Chamber allows 33 witnesses for the Stanisic Defence and 20 witnesses for the Simatovic Defence. To the extent, Mr. Bakrac, you alluded to another 15 witnesses, you would need permission for that, because we are -- at this moment we accept your request for 20 witnesses. Therefore, any further witnesses you have to file a motion and ask for additional witnesses to put on your witness list. As far as the number of hours is concerned, after having deliberated on all the arguments made, the Chamber has decided that both parties would have 70 hours for their case presentation. The Chamber adds to this that the Chamber will closely monitor and might even halfway or at one-third further evaluate on how the time is used. If, for example, you would have listed a witness for three hours and if really important, meaningful, probative, relevant evidence is presented and you would take four hours, then of course the Chamber could consider if that this would be a persistent pattern, to further hear any submissions on this same matter, but the Chamber has not gained the impression at this moment that all possibilities to improve the efficiency and to improve the performance in terms of time have been fully explored yet. The reasons for this decision will be given in writing. The Chamber wants to clearly explain to the parties why it decided as it did. Then we move on. The next item is about the Chamber's intention to move some hearings of the week to the mornings. The parties should consult the courtroom schedule for any specific days. Considering the present state of Mr. Stanisic's health and the modalities of these proceedings, the Chamber do not expect that it would cause any problems. The parties were informed of this on the 30th of May, 2011, and the Chamber would like to hear if there are any concerns in respect of this, moving some of the hearings from the afternoon to the morning. And, of course, I'm specifically looking at you, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The -- the only concern that comes to me is that I know Mr. Stanisic's health is -- is often less robust in the morning. I think it's usual that I would if I'm going in the morning to see him go after 10.00. However, I don't think that's a bar to mornings at all, but I would just ask that if there are changes or sudden fixtures in the morning that that, if at all possible, could be avoided and we could be given notice and I could just ensure that Mr. Stanisic's health is robust enough and I could make the appropriate application if it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You could -- you can look at the court schedule for -- because we'll put it on the -- on the court schedule clearly what is morning, what's afternoon. There are a few advantages of the morning. I'll not set them out in detail, but you could expect also that usually that the first session in the week, which will be most likely Tuesday or sometime perhaps Monday, would usually be the afternoon session, and then later in the week we would move to morning sessions. Is there any other observation? Other parties are -- may not be affected that directly by this. Now, before I move to the next subject, I return to one of the previous ones. Mr. Jordash, you said that for next week, and you expected you would be able to call the first witness on Tuesday and that you'd be willing to seek compensation for a lost day this week. If you would start on Tuesday, that would mean Friday. That would be Friday, the 24th of June then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that -- let me just see whether -- we have to consider whether that would be morning or afternoon. There's -- let me just check one thing. That would be most likely in the morning as I see it now. Yes. That would be -- yes. Most likely in the morning, but let me keep that open for a second. But we'd use that Friday then for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which brings me to my next agenda item, which is that -- and the parties may well be aware of that, that the Chamber has considered moving to four sitting days per week. We have done that -- considered that in the past. Now, as matters stand now, the schedule is still for three sitting days per week in accordance with the operative modalities of this trial, but the Chamber nevertheless intends to have a trial period of four sitting days per week for the fourth -- the first and the third week of July, 2011. Again, this is not a definitive change to four sittings -- sitting days per week, and we intend to proceed very cautiously in this matter, but the Chamber would like to give it a try for two weeks in July and then, but for other reasons, next week to compensate for any lost days in this week. And we would have on our mind to sit on the 4th of July in the afternoon. That's a Monday. And also to sit on the 18th of July, also a Monday. That would, therefore, be a Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday week, a four-days sitting week. We'll evaluate then what the results are. Are there any comments on this intent?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would wish to express my concern on that proposal. Whilst I would submit that the medical evidence does not in any way bar an occasional extra day, which is why I felt comfortable proposing that we make up time next week, the proposal Your Honours have put forward effectively turns the next three or four weeks into four sitting days in -- in the majority of weeks, and in our respectful submission, the medical evidence doesn't support -- or suggest that by pushing Mr. Stanisic too hard his health suffers, and I certainly have observed that when we moved to four days a week during the Prosecution case. So it's difficult. I'm not asking for relief at this time, but I can foresee a problem if we move to four days a week and its too regular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just speak to Mr. Stanisic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please -- please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic would like to address Your Honours on the subject of his health. I hadn't anticipated that, but he makes the request, and I make that on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic may address the Chamber, but before I give him an opportunity to do so, Mr. Jordash, I'm usually very carefully listening to your words. This week we have two days. Next week we have four days. The week after that we would have three days. Let me just see. Let me just have my agenda with me. Yes. Next week we would add the 24th, isn't it? Which would make this week two days, next week four days, the week after that three days, the week after that four days, the week after that three days, and the week after that four days, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I think and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How you come to a majority of the weeks with four days is -- for me it's exactly half, not a majority, and this week is only two-days week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour is right, it's not a majority, but it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have ignored the fact that one of the three-day weeks would be a two-day week. That is this week. Two, four, three, four, three, four.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not sure that it -- and I'm sure that Your Honour appreciates that it's not a case of pure arithmetics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but if you use words like a "majority," I used to understand that, and I had some difficulties understanding where the majority came from in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave it to that and let's listen to Mr. Stanisic, because that might be of the same importance. Mr. Stanisic, if you wish to stand, fine, if you would prefer to remain seated, fine as well. Just do as you wish. THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for allowing me to address you. The reason for me asking to address you lies in the following fact: Two weeks my physicians at Bronovo were at a dead regarding my further treatment. They again suggested to use the cytostatics to address my original disease. Preliminary I accepted that as I usually do when physicians make their proposals. However, upon my return to the hospital -- or, rather, to the Detention Unit, the physicians told me I had already been prescribed that treatment in Belgrade without any result. Therefore, I must tell you that you most likely did not receive all the information as to the extent of problems with my further treatment. We only have to see what any further treatment may be. If we decide to continue with the cytostatics, these are very difficult -- that's difficult medication, and during the last time they were applied I was on the verge of death. I had formerly accepted all medication, but if the physicians decide to introduce the same treatment again, I can already tell you that I will have great difficulty dealing with it. I have no idea how I'll be able to react and deal with it. This is concerning my original status without any further complication such as thrombosis in both legs and kidney problems which came as a result of that. I simply wanted to offer all available information to you so that you have it all at your disposal. I place this as a kind of hedge despite my wish to assist the speedy -- speediness of these proceedings. I am investing maximum effort to try to assist you in expediting the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanisic. First of all, the Chamber appreciates your co-operative attitude in relation to these matters. You assist us in expediting the trial. We are also aiming at expediting the trial in your own interests. It's one of the fundamental rights for an accused. It goes without saying that the Chamber carefully reads the weekly reports and any additional reports we receive. If there's any specific information which is not contained in the weekly reports, then of course the Chamber would certainly insist on being as complete as possible in that respect, and hearing with that we might not have been provided with the full information, of course, is of some concern to us and we will give that some follow-up. If a change in medication or any other relevant aspect of the treatment would -- would not favour our plans, then of course we'll carefully consider whether we should, nevertheless, do this test or not. But of course, it's difficult to say anything about not having been provided with the information. And do not hesitate either to request to directly address the Chamber on these matters, or ask Mr. Jordash's assistance in dealing with these matters. What we're trying to do is find a fair balance between fairly considering your health situation and, at the same time, to provide a trial which is expeditious not only for the Tribunal purposes but also because it's a fundamental right for you. Thank you for that. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I understood correctly, and I hope I did not interrupt you, I believed you were complete in your comments to what Mr. Stanisic said. As regards morning or afternoon sessions, our Defence did not have a position. It is all the same to us when we sit, and, of course, we take seriously into account what Mr. Jordash said as to Mr. Stanisic's ability to follow the proceedings and his condition being better in the afternoon. We do not object to that. As for -- as regards the number of sitting days, we realise that the basic problem of this trial is the health situation of Mr. Stanisic. In view of that, I'd like to ask you to consider another possibility. A moment ago I told you that our Defence is intensely working on the completion of our investigation. Why do we want that? So that we could forward all the material to the Prosecution depending -- pending your approval to supplement our 65 ter list. We want to do that so as to allow the Prosecution enough time to prepare for our Defence case. That is why we would prefer if the trial period came later, following the summer recess, so that we could use the time before the recess to conclude our investigation to the extent possible, thus enabling the Prosecutor to get acquainted with all our evidence and material. That is why it would be useful for us to remain with this sitting schedule until the summer break. It would mean a lot to us. It would mean that each week we would have an extra day that we could use towards completing our investigation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Each week would mean in this respect two days altogether. Yes. Well, it's -- it's -- it's saying the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in different words. Each week another day or two days until the summer recess, but the -- I would say the psychological meaning of the two expressions is slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't do my math, it seems. You are quite correct, Your Honour. It is actually three or four days. In any case, in the situation we are in, those three or four days would mean a lot. You are fully correct. I did say every week, and yet I failed to notice that you said every other week. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from that, three or four days would be two or three days, but let's get rid of the mathematics. Prosecution, any comment on --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll consider the submissions made by Mr. Jordash, Mr. Stanisic, and Mr. Bakrac, and we will inform the parties accordingly. Next on my agenda, translation difficulties. We've heard already some about it. I do understand that there was a common effort and with some support of Chambers staff to see whether translations could be prioritised and could be -- could be produced as quickly as possible. We also understood that quite some progress was made, but if there's anything apart from what has been said before that should be added, then the parties have an opportunity to do so. Mr. Jordash, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Some progress has been made, but not -- and I speak on behalf of the Prosecution and the Defence, not sufficient for either party to feel terribly comfortable with the amount outstanding. We've agreed with the Prosecution that we will provide the Prosecution with a greater notice concerning which exhibits we will use with the forthcoming witnesses, and we will send them a list next week to cover the first four witnesses. It won't be precise, but it will be, I hope, of assistance, and then we will sit down with the Prosecution next week to work out what translations are outstanding, whether the amount outstanding is going to be a problem for either of us, and if it's a problem, it may be that we turn to Your Honours to seek relief by way of a joint motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will see with these matters -- how these matters develop. You may be aware that the Chamber has always tried to give its full support to -- to prioritise translations for this case. I also understand that CLSS has -- is really trying to do its utmost best, but where it all ends and where we face difficulties which are difficult to handle and to manage is -- is still to be seen. I'd rather not speculate too much about it and, rather, show full awareness of the problems that may arise in the near future as already explained also by Ms. Marcus. At the same time, to go into details at this moment seems not to be very useful. It could be that some documents untranslated that for other reasons you would decide not to use them, which would perhaps result in you not asking for a delay of cross-examination on those matters. I'm not confident that we will resolve all the problems, but we also -- we should not try to cross bridges until we come to them. We see that in our road there are a few bridges nearby. I'm aware of that. Let's see how the situation is as we have proceeded. Mr. Jordash, you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just make one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We share the Prosecution's concern. It's frustrating for us, and we feel slight -- somewhat hampered by the volume -- I certainly feel hampered because I can't read some of the exhibits and I have to have a legal assistant take me through that exhibit, and would I prefer to have the documents translated. So it's -- it's a problem which I -- we've thought about a lot, and we've thought very seriously coming to Your Honours for ourselves. So we are keeping that in mind, and we are very close to doing that, because we -- we don't want to advance a case with exhibits on a list that presenting counsel hasn't had the opportunity to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd said if you can't cross the bridge, what about the Prosecution? They certainly would not, but the first thing is that you have to cross the bridge as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'd like to cross before they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I understand that. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour just to point out one thing. I agree with what Mr. Jordash said. Just to give the Chamber a sense of the magnitude of the problem: As of this morning, we counted on a spreadsheet the number of outstanding translations into B/C/S and that totals 1.108 documents out of approximately 4.000 on their list. So it -- regardless of how we try to get across the bridges, I think we do -- we do face very serious translation issues. I just wanted to put that -- that number on the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It now is on the record. Now, you are referring to outstanding translations into B/C/S, I take it, from English?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that at least Mr. Jordash can read those documents, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Into English from B/C/S. Please forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You see, I really trying to carefully listen to whatever your submissions you make. Okay. Then all these remarks I had on my mind, I'll forget about them. It's clear it's for the Chamber to take care that we all cross the river without getting wet feet, and we'll pay attention to that. The next item I have on my list is -- and I think we can deal with them in open session, is the request for protective measures -- Serbia's request for protective measures, 26 of November, 2010 and the 8th of April, 2011. These were documents that were provided to you, Mr. Jordash, I think, in redacted form, and you meanwhile received -- you received instructions that you should deal with those -- with those documents as confidential documents; that is, that you would have to move into private session -- at least request to the Chamber to move into private session when the documents are used in court, and if you want to tender them for admission, that you should do -- do so provisionally under seal. Now, we understood that -- initially we understood that you had been provided only with redacted copies of those documents but that you would be provided with unredacted copies and that you meanwhile received those. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't think that is correctly understood. I -- I'm not aware of the National Council disclosing -- sorry, not disclosing but corresponding with us and informing us that BIA has reversed their position on any of the redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact, but perhaps we should check that, that in the -- the motion which was filed on the 26th of November, 2010, that the Republic of Serbia had specified that they would provide the Stanisic Defence with unredacted copies without delay if the use of unredacted documents is necessary for the proceedings. And that's what is found in their --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then they've -- they communicated with us, and I'll have to check the -- whether they are discussing the same document, but the latest communication we received from the National Council was that none of the redactions are, in fact, relevant to our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's still that same problem. We're talking about the same documents at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think so, and it's -- it's National Council -- or I should say BIA via the National Council who are making the assessment of what they say is relevant to our case. So it's somewhat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check whether -- whether we really find, and I don't have that motion here at this very moment, that you'd be provided with unredacted copies without delay if the use of unredacted documents is necessary for the proceedings, and, of course, what is necessary for the proceedings is to be judged by the parties and by the Chamber. And if the Prosecution opposes admission of any document, if there are redactions, then of course it's in your own interest as well. We'll further look at this and we have to pay specific attention to that. Let me see. And we also should be aware that, of course, protective measures are primarily to keep away information from the public rather than from the parties or from the Chamber. And if there are any specific concerns there, of course, there are procedures to deal with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well -- well, Your Honour, I would completely agree. I mean, paragraph 3 of the 24 of September 2010 Serbian request seems to be somewhat unhelpful or in light of the letter we received recently whereby the Republic of Serbia say, "We are maintaining redactions," then it may be that the right approach is for me to right now simply say I invite the Chamber to order the National Council to unredact the documents so that we can make a decision rather than the decision resting in their hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm hesitant to do this, but in order to have a clear situation, might it not be better to make such an application in writing? I know that it's an additional burden for you, but nevertheless, in these sensitive matters it might be better to have a short and clear history.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The only problem I can foresee is that we cannot, of course -- it's slightly circular in that we can't say it is relevant, because we don't know what's there. We can only say it's relevant inasmuch as it's part of a document we want to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you can write down, of course, is from a point of view of fair proceedings that it should not be left -- the relevance of certain materials should not be left in the hands of a party that provides that information where there's a general duty to provide information, either documentary evidence or witness testimony. And the mere fact that you do not know and that the Chamber doesn't know means that we are all a bit handicapped. And perhaps there are ways if there are specific concerns, not relevance, but other concerns covered by Rule 54 bis, then of course there are solutions for that as well, but I do not see that that has been invoked at this moment. I do understand that in the letter -- you'll find the letter, which of course we haven't seen, and if you make a written submission you could refer to that letter, and of course otherwise it would just be what you tell us now and I have no reason not to believe it, but it's a bad basis for us to issue an order upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm wondering, Your Honour, whether the right approach might be that we -- we go back to the National Council and say, "Well, why do you arrive at that position?" Or, "What -- can you explain what it is is the basis for your view that it should remain private, "or else we are perhaps not quite understanding why they've may the decision other than they'd rather not disclose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a matter of fact, that what would be preferable is a road which leads to a resolution as quickly as possible.
