That's -- and, of course, the Chamber at this moment, unless -- if the parties would reach a position where they say, "We can't take any further initiative," then of course you have to address the Chamber. Don't wait too long to address the Chamber. If you can resolve the matters by yourself, fine, but don't try to do that so that we are running out of time in July, September, October, November in discussions. Let's get to the core of the problem as quickly as possible, and if one first initial step you think would help, then take that step and then address it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To be honest, not to take up too much time, the -- our view is that the best approach is for the Prosecution to do it for this reason: that we are having trouble with the National Council. We have sent a number of requests over the months and the years, and we do and have -- sorry, we have arrived at the view that they prefer to co-operate with the Prosecution. Now, I think if the Prosecution were to either apply or we do a joint application - we're not against that - we might get more from such an approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A joint application, of course, would underline the importance of receiving the appropriate material. Ms. Marcus, any observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would just -- we have nothing -- we're not opposed to, I think, a joint submission on the issue. If the Stanisic Defence has the correspondence, so as soon as they put it together into a motion, we're perfectly happy to -- to agree to that. They can send us a draft and we'll be happy to do that. I would note it is quite a matter of some urgency due to the fact that there are 36 redacted documents on the list for the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That also explains why I said let's -- let's try to find a way which quickest leads to -- to a result.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, we cannot exclude under all circumstances that you might not be able to finish the cross-examination or that you'd have to reserve the right to recall a witness for further cross-examination. That's -- it has happened before in this Tribunal. It has happened before in this Chamber -- before this Chamber. That's reality. At the same time to wait and first resolve everything before we proceed would have also some disadvantages, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, we have a pending application for the delay of the cross-examination of the first witness for that reason and a number of others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, and you may also be aware that the Chamber often prefer to see how far we can come, and then to consider whether there be any need for a recall for further cross-examination, but we will consider that. It also depends on what happens Thursday. Then next item also deals with protective measures. On the 3rd of November in 2009, the Chamber partially granted a request for Serbia for protective measures ordering that the names of active BIA members on certain documents provided by Serbia should receive protective measures, and in order to give effect to this order, the Chamber ordered Serbia to give a list of the active BIA members appearing on the documents covered by the request and to be given to the Prosecution. On the 8th of December, 2009, the Prosecution confirmed that it had received such a list. The Prosecution is hereby invited to provide the Chamber with a copy of this list, and the Chamber will take care that the Republic of Serbia is informed about this request to the Prosecution to avoid any misunderstandings and to ensure full transparency.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I move to my next item, which is about, if I could say so, the Theunens documents. On the 1st of April of this year, the Chamber admitted a number of documents into evidence, namely P1049, P1065, P1069, P1159, P1163, P1181, and P1412. They related to the testimony of the witness Theunens, and the documents were admitted on the condition that revised translations were provided within 20 days of rendering of that decision. The Prosecution now provided translations, but most of the requested translations were received after the 20-day deadline. More specifically, they were received on the 12th of May, 2011. However, the Chamber accepts this late submission and thereby affirms the admission decision and requests the Registry to make the necessary replacement in e-court. The next item on my agenda is the slides used during the Rule 98 bis submissions. The Prosecution has used three documents which were subsequently marked for identification as P2973 up to and include P2975. These were parts of the Prosecution submission, and they do not qualify in themselves as evidence. Accordingly, the Chamber finds it more appropriate to have these documents filed by the Prosecution as opposed to having them added to the body of evidence in this case. P2973, 74, and 75 are denied admission, and the Prosecution is instructed to file these documents within ten days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. The next item is a request which the Chamber will declare moot. On the 27th of May of this year, the Chamber issued its decision on the Prosecution's urgent motion for disclosure of witness details and for modification of the Scheduling Order of the 1st of April 2011. Prior to the decision being distributed but after it had been filed with the Registry, the Prosecution's request for leave to reply was distributed. As the Chamber has decided the motion, the request for leave to reply is moot. The next item, I'd like to put on the record that on the 7th of June, 2011, the Chamber issued a confidential decision in which it granted a Prosecution request for re-opening of its case. It admitted one document into evidence and exclusively for the confidential character of the one document admitted into evidence it was that the Chamber has decided to file this decision confidentially, not to say that re-opening of the case is not something the public should not know about. It's exclusively the content of the document admitted into evidence which caused the Chamber to make this a confidential decision. I move to the next item on my agenda which is the request by Mr. Karadzic access two confidential Defence materials. On the 31st of May of this year, Radovan Karadzic filed a motion before this Chamber requesting that the Stanisic and Simatovic Defence comply with the Chamber's decision of the 16th of July 2009, almost two years ago, and identify to the Registry all inter partes confidential Defence exhibits and filings. On the 16th of July, 2009, the Chamber had partially granted Karadzic access to such materials. Mr. Jordash and Mr. Bakrac, today is the final day to respond to this motion. Could you tell us -- could you tell the Chamber what your positions are?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we have a little time to respond? Not a great deal of time, but if we could have a couple of weeks, we would be able to identify and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're saying, as a matter of fact, is that your response is that you would need more time to comply with the order and that you're asking for that time, which is different from a response to the motion. The motion would be, "It's not true. We did comply." Apparently, I do understand that the Stanisic Defence admits that it has not complied with the order and requests for more time to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We confess completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Mr. Bakrac, another confession or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I confess. I share Mr. Jordash's position. You know what the reasons were for that. We were focused on preparing our own Defence, and we're going to do our very best to comply and do our part of the work involved, but we also kindly ask you for additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time you think you would need? Mr. Jordash asked for a couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, we also need two weeks at least for that. We don't want to be the "enfant terrible" in this case, and we don't want to ask for even more time, so we'll try to do what we have to do within those two weeks that Mr. Jordash had requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I understood a couple of weeks, perhaps even a bit more than two weeks, but let's -- 12th of July. Would that be a solution for -- 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac as well. Then the Stanisic and the Simatovic Defence are hereby ordered to comply with the 16th of July, 2009 decision and inform the Chamber through a filing by the 12th of July, 2011, what material you have identified so far to the Registry. And, Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to inform Mr. Karadzic of this ruling. I move to my next agenda item. I'm a bit in doubt as to when to take a break, because we started late. Mr. Stanisic might have been waiting in this courtroom for 15 minutes for our return. I have two more items on my agenda, and the last one whether there are any other matters to be raised by the parties. If there's any need to take a break, we'll do so. Then expert reports. The Simatovic Defence has requested an extension for the submission of two expert reports. The suggestion was that the English versions of the report would be disclosed on the 12th of August. The Prosecution apparently took no position on this proposed deadline, although in that same response you expressed the concerns we discussed earlier about the -- shifting the Defence case, which we have sufficiently dealt with. I'm asking the Stanisic Defence whether you would have any problem with the Simatovic Defence filing the two reports by the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We're in a similar position. We expect to file our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll come to your expert report soon, Mr. Jordash. Now, Mr. Simatovic, we noted that in your 65 ter summaries why -- we do not find much on your expert, apart that one is a police expert and the other one a military expert. At the same time, in your 6th of June motion in which you ask for an extension of time, we find detailed information about the expert report we could expect from Mr. Milosevic. However, not much about the report we'll receive in relation to Mr. Borojevic. We do not know much than that it's a military expert. Is there anyway that you could provide additional information both on the expert himself, a CV, and a short summary of what we could expect in relation to his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, or if you think that it would be more convenient that way, perhaps during the course of today or tomorrow morning I can submit the contents, and Mr. Borovic's CV in writing. If you think that is better, then I could do that. If I were to supposed to speak about it now, I'd have to find all the relevant material. As far as the military expert is concerned, he was a joint expert on the list of the previous Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't that true that you have explained all this in your 6th of June motion in which you asked for an extension of time? So therefore the Chamber is familiar with what you raised there. If you would kind enough to file the CV and a summary of what we could expect as the subject matter of the report is concerned, well, within, well, let's say, still this week, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I shall do my best to do it as soon as possible. If you would allow me just one more minute. How did we get to this estimate of the 12th of July for all -- or, rather, the 12th of August to have all the translations? We asked our experts to finish their reports by the beginning of the summer recess, the 23rd of July. We have their promises that that would -- that that is indeed what they would do, and we assume that the CLSS can have that translated from the 23rd of July until the 12th of August. If an additional day or two is required by CLSS, please take that into account, because that is the deadline that we had assumed would be doable in terms of having these expert reports translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, don't work too much on the basis of assumptions, apparently you assume that CLSS could do the job in a month. You apparently also assume that CLSS would need no holidays; whereas, most other people would need some time to relax. So therefore, I would urge you not to assume anything but to get in touch with CLSS and to see how realistic your assumptions are. I'm also saying this in view of having looked at the table of contents of the Milosevic report. I could imagine that they need half a year, because it's six or seven pages just listing the chapters of that report. So therefore I think since the report is not yet ready, perhaps executive summaries at the beginning of chapters so as to be able to work already on the matter. I'm really a bit concerned if which -- about such a report which seems to be so extensive that, to work on the basis of assumptions, usurping more or less the holidays of CLSS, it seems to be a risky exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, if you allow me, the assumption only has to do with this translation. I am sorry you reminded me now of something that I had not actually mentioned. Actually, Mr. Petrovic and I asked Mr. Milosevic the expert to provide chapters of his report as he finishes them so that we can submit them for translation; that is to say, before the final version is done. We had that in mind, so we asked the expert to do that. I agree that on the basis of the contents it seems enormous. However, we have firm assurances from Dr. Milosevic that he can finish this by the 23rd and we indeed had envisaged that possibility, namely, as soon as he finishes one chapter, he sends it to us, and then we send it for translation. That is perhaps why we came up with this optimistic forecast of the 12th of August, to have it all translated by then, because it would have been too optimistic, I believe, if we had submitted all of it only on the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I saw that the index of the content is in English, but do I take it that the report will produced in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In order to be as expeditious as possible, we actually translated this for the Prosecution so that we could provide as much information as possible. We had done that in order to give the Prosecution as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we receive -- within the next day we receive a summary of the report of Mr. Borovic and his CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we shall do that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I promise that had we -- that we would come to your experts soon. When do you intend to file the proposed expert report, because I do understand that it will be only Mr. Browne's expert report. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At the moment, that is all we are certain that we will file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's almost impossible to say at the moment. If I can just tell Your Honour why. Mr. Browne's going to examine the so-called Mladic diaries. In order to do that, we have to go through the Prosecution, who have provided some restrictions on what we can do with the diaries, which has taken some time to iron out. Mr. Browne now has to come to The Hague. We now have another problem, which is where he can examine them, and the problem with that is that the Prosecution insists that he has to go to a particular lab, a forensic laboratory, to look at them. OLAD are saying they're not willing to pay that. We now have to go back to the Prosecution. To cut a long story short, all the administrative requirements have taken over, I think, six weeks now, and all that he has been able to do is give them a preliminary examination. So we still haven't got the funding. We still haven't worked out precisely where he can examine them. Once that's worked out, and I would hope that's organised in the next two to three weeks at the most, although we may have to come to Your Honours if OLAD will not provide the funding. Mr. Browne then want up to a month to be able to do his examinations and thereafter write his report. So writing the report is in additional to month. And then at that point we can serve it on the parties. So at least two months, I would estimate, and maybe more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to give the Prosecution position on this. The Prosecution has tried or endeavoured to accommodate Mr. Jordash's request and in most cases has within 24 hours obtained the information that it needed to answer his request. The Prosecution is forming its views about what can be done to the books in consultation with experts at the Dutch forensic institute. They have made their facility available, a room that can ensure that the books aren't contaminated. So it's really a minimal requirement. With respect to the tests that have been requested, the Prosecution has already agreed that it would not object and would facilitate any examination of the books that did not have a possibility of causing deterioration or damage to the books. There is one particular test that Mr. Browne wishes to conduct which, on the advice of the experts at the Dutch forensic institute, the Netherlands Forensic Institute, could cause damage to the books. So the Prosecution's position is that we cannot consent to that. Of course, Mr. Jordash, if he's able to obtain an order from the Trial Chamber requiring us to do that, we would abide by any order, but we don't see that we can properly consent to jeopardising the integrity of the books absent an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We were not intend to criticize the Prosecution. The long and short of it is is that the Prosecution insists that the books have to be examined in the -- I forget the name of the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nederlands Forensisch Instituut.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I couldn't even have said it if I'd known it, and it costs 160 euros an hour, and Mr. Browne wants to examine it -- these books over a month, and OLAD are saying no way, and so Mr. Browne says, "Well I don't need to use the laboratory. I can examine them in the court. Their facilities are sufficient to maintain the integrity of the books." We're going to ask the Prosecution therefore to pay for the laboratory. So that's the position we're in at the moment because otherwise we don't have the funding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the Chamber can assist in resolving this matter, of course we'll be glad to do so. I don't know to what extent the expert needs the facilities of the -- I mean to sit in a laboratory to read a law book may be expensive and not very efficient. I do not know to what extent the expert needs the facilities of the laboratory in that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, he's saying he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What he's -- what he's going to do is conduct -- he's basically examining them to see if they've been altered or written chronologically or whether there's any evidence that they'd been doctored which is what we say has occurred, and Mr. Browne is looking at them through infra-red and various other techniques which examine the paper at close hand, and he's saying, "Well, I think the facilities at the court are sufficient," and the Prosecution are saying, "Well, we'd like you to go to that laboratory. " Because our expert -- I think their expert says they should be examined there. So it's a battle between the experts at the moment, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. Mr. Weber, you're an expert on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, not a forensic document examiner. Your Honour, at this moment the parties have not had any communications regarding the topic that's being brought up by Mr. Jordash. There's been no proposal for any other location, as far as the Prosecution is aware, aside from the Netherlands Forensic Institute. So there's actually -- not aware at this time what Mr. Jordash is talking about. Of course, you know, these are notebooks that are in the possession and custody of the Office of the Prosecutor, so we do have to maintain some custody over these notebooks and any testing that would occur. So that is the main consideration that we have had at this time along with any information that the Stanisic Defence could provide us would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hardly can imagine that no secure environment could be found, whether or not, for example, with video surveillance so as to see that nothing happens to the originals. Of course, the experts being able to write down whatever notes he wants outside the scope of any camera so as not to follow what he is writing. And I hardly can imagine that no solution could be found for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be clear, Counsel's requested access to inspect the notebooks pursuant to 66(B) to conduct forensic testing. So there has to be a location that can -- can facilitate the forensic testing that the Defence has [indiscernible] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So the court -- the courtroom building is probably not a location where the requested forensic testing could occur and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly why I asked whether the facilities of the laboratory were needed. Now, infra-red is not, I think, something you need necessarily a laboratory environment to use that, and apparently he brings his own equipment. I can imagine that you want to look at that equipment first to see what kind of equipment it is, to check all that, and then find a secured, even perhaps an environment under surveillance where it could always be verified at a later stage whether anything was done to the original material which was inappropriate. I really can't imagine that you do not find a solution for this problem. Eight times 160 euros a day, that is a thousand for one month. That's well over -- I don't know whether he takes any holidays, yes or no, but I can't imagine that it cannot be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, and you're correct, it's just that we -- this has not been the conversation up until now, and I don't want to waste the Chamber's time, we will discuss this. We were always under the impression that this expert wanted to use the ESDL machine which is a very high-tech piece of equipment which exists only in the Netherlands Forensic Institute and that's part of the reason why. The other reason was to have a facility that would preserve any trace evidence on the books, but we can -- we can create a -- a sterile environment here in the building and we have done that already for those notebooks. So I'm happy to discuss this further with Mr. Jordash, and if he does not seek to use any of the equipment at the Netherlands Forensic Institute, it may very well be that we can accommodate his request to do it in this building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if my observations have brought this matter one step further, I'm happy and that I hope that others will take the next steps. The Chamber would like to be informed as soon as possible if this discussion ends up in a deadlock, because that's what we cannot afford. We'll then also set a time limit. I had on my mind the 15th of August and then of course Dr. Browne could then take his holidays after that, but I'm not the master of his family holidays. Could you please keep Chamber's staff informed about any progress made in this respect on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move to what is on my -- the last item on my agenda, which is -- yes, whether the Prosecution's 65 ter documents should retain their 65 ter numbers or whether new numbers should be given to them. I do understand that the Registry has no specific preference, neither has the Chamber. The risk of confusion is, I think, biggest if they were provided with new numbers, so therefore the suggestion, although we have no clear preference, but just in order to avoid any errors in the near future is to just not give them new numbers, but again we have no strong feelings about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Our preference is to keep the old numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that's how we will proceed. Let me just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My last question is whether there's any matter to the -- the parties would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, five minutes if you will allow me and if Mr. Stanisic can take it. Just two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear that if Mr. Stanisic would prefer to have a break then, but it also depends on how much time you would need, Mr. Jordash, because if that would be another 20 minutes, then, of course, we would have to take a break anyhow and I'd rather do it now. How much time -- how much time do you need, Mr. Jordash? Do you need any time at all to raise any further matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we are talking about five minutes only, and I do understand from Mr. Stanisic that he would not insist on having a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to hurry with this so that we can be done as soon as possible for Mr. Stanisic's sake. According to Rule 54, we address the Trial Chamber with a request. I think that we are in private session because this is confidential. No, we're not. Can we please prove into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber has nothing else on its agenda. The Prosecution has no further issues to raise; Mr. Jordash, you had nothing; we have heard the submissions by Mr. Bakrac, which means that this concludes this Pre-Defence Conference. We will adjourn until tomorrow, Wednesday, the 15th of June, 9.00 in the morning, and we will then hear the opening statement by the Stanisic Defence. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
